extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy, and scientific inquiry; general educated readers interested in methods of reasoning and evidence
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and canons for judging the correctness of inference, the sufficiency of evidence, and the auxiliary operations (naming, definition, classification) that facilitate scientific investigation and reasoning. Emphasis on induction as part of reasoning and on limits of logic relative to intuition/metaphysics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition should define the scope of inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: To define, is to select from among all the properties of a thing, those which shall be understood to be designated and declared by its name; as much as is to be expected from a definition placed at the commencement of a subject, is that it should define the scope of our inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions should indicate the scope and purpose of the investigation rather than attempt finality; they must be based on well-known particulars and are properly progressive—revised as the science advances (examples: chemistry, biology). Avoid treating an opening definition as the final or exhaustive account of the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic = science + art of reasoning (analysis + rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is the Science, as well as the Art, of reasoning; meaning by the former term, the analysis of the mental process which takes place whenever we reason, and by the latter, the rules, grounded on that analysis, for conducting the process correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory treatment of logic must both analyze how inference operates and derive practical canons from that analysis. Art presupposes knowledge: rules should be grounded in correct analysis of the mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the wide sense of 'reasoning' to include induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoning ... in the wider signification ... to infer any assertion from assertions already admitted: and in this sense, induction is as much entitled to be called reasoning as the demonstrations of geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not restrict evaluation of reasoning to syllogistic deduction alone; include inductive inference from particulars to generals when judging correctness and sufficiency of arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish intuition (consciousness) from inference; logic concerns inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is not the science of Belief, but the science of Proof, or Evidence. With the claims which any proposition has to belief on the evidence of consciousness—that is, without evidence in the proper sense of the word—logic has nothing to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not evaluate immediate, intuitive truths (conscious sensations, direct perception) using logical canons; logic's task is to judge beliefs asserted on the basis of evidence or inference. Beware of mistaking rapid inferences for intuition (e.g., perception of distance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic judges sufficiency of evidence; it does not find evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic, however, is not the same thing with knowledge, though the field of logic is co-extensive with the field of knowledge. Logic does not undertake to find evidence, but to determine whether it has been found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an investigation, separate the empirical work (observation, experiment, discovery of facts) from the logical assessment: logic tests whether the available facts meet the relations required to constitute proof of a conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations of naming, definition, and classification are subsidiary to induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic includes the operation of Naming; for language is an instrument of thought... It includes, also, Definition, and Classification... These are operations specially instrumental to the estimation of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of scientific work should include whether terminology, definitions, and classification appropriately marshal facts to make evidence accessible and reduce chances of error (i.e., clarity, stability, and usefulness of concepts matter for reasoning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze inference only as far as required for practical judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall attempt to analyze the process of inference ... so far only as may be requisite for ascertaining the difference between a correct and an incorrect performance of those processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not demand excessively deep metaphysical or psychological decomposition of mental faculties when evaluating reasoning; analysis should go as far as necessary to reveal errors or correctness in performance, no further. This is an anti-pattern against over-refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic prescribes relations between data and conclusions that must be observed
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic points out what relations must subsist between data and whatever can be concluded from them, between proof and every thing which it can prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should check whether the necessary relations (e.g., relevancy, sufficiency, appropriateness of scope) between premises/observations and claimed conclusions are present. Look for indispensable conditions that determine valid proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canons for testing sufficiency of evidence (logic as art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our object, then, will be, to attempt a correct analysis of the intellectual process called Reasoning or Inference ... as well as, on the foundation of this analysis, and pari passu with it, to bring together or frame a set of rules or canons for testing the sufficiency of any given evidence to prove any given proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critiquing work, apply explicit canons derived from analysis (e.g., criteria for induction, standards for causal inference, checks for generalization). The text promises concrete rules (later chapters) such as the methods of experimental inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse logic with metaphysical questions about origins of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic must be restricted to that portion of our knowledge which consists of inferences from truths previously known; ... With the original data, or ultimate premises of our knowledge; with their number or nature, the mode in which they are obtained, or the tests by which they may be distinguished; logic, in a direct way at least, has nothing to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating arguments, avoid conflating logical sufficiency with debates about whether premises are innate, metaphysically justified, or the product of psychology—those belong to other disciplines (metaphysics, psychology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical instruction increases reliability and progress of inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: There are limits both to what mechanicians can do without principles of mechanics, and to what thinkers can do without principles of logic. ... A few individuals ... may work without principles ... But the bulk of mankind require either to understand the theory of what they are doing, or to have rules laid down for them by those who have understood the theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate educational and methodological aspects: good training in logical canons is a criterion of likely quality and progress in scientific work; absence of explicit logical standards is a weakness except in rare genius cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and conceptual apparatus must be responsive to the science's needs
rubrics_metrics.description: The earlier chapters ... will consequently appear, to some readers, needlessly elementary and scholastic. But those who know in what darkness the nature of our knowledge ... is often involved by a confused apprehension of the import of the different classes of Words and Assertions, will not regard these discussions as either frivolous, or irrelevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether conceptual groundwork (elementary distinctions, classification schemes) is adequate and justified for the subject-matter; apparent pedantry may be warranted if it removes confusion that would vitiate evidence or inference.
